q: other and y are bound to the same objects as name and x. Then name and x are changed with +=. What does this print?
code:
name = "ann"
other = name
name += "e"

x = 10
y = x
x += 1
print(other, y)
why: Strings and ints are immutable, so += cannot change the object in place. It builds a new object and rebinds name and x to it. other and y still refer to the original "ann" and 10.
wrong: The names share objects at first, but += on an immutable value makes a new object, so other and y keep the old ones.
Strings are immutable just like ints, so name += "e" makes a new string and other keeps "ann".
x += 1 rebinds x to a new int 11; y is still bound to 10.

q: In Python, variables hold references to objects; for lists, + creates a new list whereas += extends the list in place. What does this print?
why: a + [3] builds a new list and rebinds a to it, so b still sees the old [1, 2]. For a list, c += [3] extends the existing object in place, so d, which names that same object, sees [1, 2, 3].
wrong: a = a + [3] does not touch the original list; it creates a new one and moves only the name a.
+= on a list mutates it in place, unlike on ints and strings, so the alias d sees the change.
This swaps the two behaviours: + makes a new list, while += changes the existing one.

q: b is a slice copy of a list of lists. One inner list is changed through b, and one slot of b is replaced. What does this print?
code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a[:]
b[0].append(9)
b[1] = [7]
print(a)
print(b)
why: a[:] copies only the outer list, and both outer lists hold the same two inner lists. b[0].append(9) changes a shared inner list, so a sees it. b[1] = [7] only rebinds a slot in b's own outer list, so a keeps [2].
wrong: That is a deep copy. A slice copies the outer list but shares the inner lists, so the append shows in a.
b is a new outer list, not another name for a, so replacing b[1] does not touch a.
This flips the levels: a shallow copy gets its own outer list and shares the inner ones, not the other way round.

q: A test needs its own copy of a nested settings dict, like {"db": {"port": 5432}}, so it can change any value without touching the original. Which line gives that?
options: test_cfg = {k: v for k, v in cfg.items()}
why: deepcopy copies the outer dict and, recursively, every dict and list nested inside it. The test can then change test_cfg["db"]["port"] while the original keeps 5432.
wrong: Assignment only binds a second name to the same dict, so every change hits the original.
copy() is shallow: the outer dict is new, but cfg["db"] is the same inner dict in both.
The comprehension builds a new outer dict but reuses the same values, so the inner dict is still shared.

q: In Python, list * n repeats the list's existing element references n times, while [expr for _ in range(n)] evaluates expr once per iteration. Two 3 x 3 grids are built and modified. What does this print?
code:
grid = [[0] * 3] * 3
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)

rows = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
rows[0][0] = 1
print(rows)
why: [[0] * 3] * 3 repeats a reference to one inner list three times, so every row is the same object and the change shows in each. The comprehension runs [0] * 3 once per row, making three separate lists.
wrong: * 3 on the outer list copies references, not rows, so the first grid has one shared row.
The comprehension evaluates [0] * 3 on every pass, so its rows are separate lists.
This is reversed: the * 3 version shares one row, and the comprehension makes new ones.

q: update appends to its argument, then assigns a new list to the parameter and appends again. What does this print?
code:
def update(items):
    items.append(4)
    items = [0]
    items.append(5)

data = [1, 2, 3]
update(data)
print(data)
why: The parameter items starts as another name for data, so append(4) changes the caller's list. items = [0] only rebinds the local name to a new list; append(5) goes to that new list, which is then thrown away.
wrong: Python passes a reference to the same list, not a copy, so the first append is visible to the caller.
Assigning to a parameter rebinds the local name only; it cannot replace the caller's variable.
After items = [0], the name no longer refers to data, so append(5) changes only the new list.

q: A tuple holds a string and a list. The code appends to the list, then tries to replace the string. What does this print?
code:
point = ("p1", [1, 2])
point[1].append(3)
print(point)
try:
    point[0] = "p2"
except TypeError:
    print("TypeError")
options: Nothing: the append raises TypeError first
('p1', [1, 2, 3]) only, since point[0] can be reassigned
why: A tuple fixes which objects it holds, not what happens inside them. The list in slot 1 is mutable, so append works and the tuple shows [1, 2, 3]. Assigning to point[0] tries to change the tuple itself, which raises TypeError.
wrong: The tuple only stops its slots from being replaced; the list it holds can still be changed.
The tuple holds a reference to the list, not a frozen copy, so it shows the appended 3.
Tuples do not support item assignment, so point[0] = "p2" raises TypeError.

q: In Python, default parameter expressions are evaluated once when def runs and stored on the function object. add_tag is called twice using the default and once with []. What does this print?
code:
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("a"))
print(add_tag("b"))
print(add_tag("c", []))
options: SyntaxError: a default value cannot be a list
why: The default list is created once, when def runs, and every call that leaves out tags reuses that one list. So the second call appends to the list that already holds 'a'. The third call passes its own list, so it starts empty.
wrong: Defaults are not rebuilt on each call; the same list object is reused, so 'a' is still in it.
Passing a list replaces the default for that call, so the shared list is not involved.
Any object can be a default value. Python allows mutable defaults, which is why this bug is common.

q: In Python, a default parameter expression is evaluated when def executes and stored on the function object. What does this print?
code:
limit = 10

def check(value, max_value=limit):
    return value <= max_value

limit = 100
print(check(50))
options: NameError: limit is not defined inside check
TypeError: a default must be a literal
why: A default value is computed once, when the def statement runs. At that moment limit is 10, so max_value defaults to 10 for good. Rebinding limit to 100 later does not change the stored default, and 50 <= 10 is False.
wrong: The default is not looked up again on each call, so the later limit = 100 is not seen.
limit already exists when the def runs, so the default is computed without error.
Any expression can be a default; it is just evaluated once, at definition time.

q: In Python, lambda: expr defines a closure that looks up outer variables in the enclosing scope when called, and a for loop shares one loop variable in that scope. What does this print?
code:
handlers = []
for i in range(3):
    handlers.append(lambda: i * 10)

print([h() for h in handlers])
options: NameError: i is gone after the loop
why: Each lambda looks up i when it is called, not when it is created. By then the loop has finished and i is 2, so all three return 20. Binding the value at creation, for example lambda i=i: i * 10, gives [0, 10, 20].
wrong: That needs each lambda to capture the value; here they share the variable i and read it later.
range(3) stops at 2, so the last value i takes is 2, not 3.
A loop variable stays defined after the loop ends, so the lambdas can still read it.

q: increment reads and updates the module-level count with +=. What happens when it is called?
code:
count = 0

def increment():
    count += 1
    return count

print(increment())
options: It prints 1 and the global count stays 0
why: Because count is assigned inside increment, Python treats count as local for the whole function. count += 1 then reads that local before it has a value. Declaring global count inside the function makes it use the module variable.
wrong: Reading a global works, but assigning to it in a function makes the name local unless it is declared global.
Nothing is returned: count += 1 fails on its read, before the return line runs.
Python does not start a local copy from the global value; the read fails before any addition.

q: make_counter sets n = 0 and returns an inner function that runs n += 1 and returns n. Calling the returned inner function raises UnboundLocalError. What fixes it and keeps the count across calls?
options: Declare nonlocal n in the inner function
Declare global n in the inner function
Move n = 0 into the inner function, before n += 1
Rename n so it does not clash with anything
why: n += 1 assigns n, so Python treats n as local to the inner function. nonlocal n says that n belongs to the enclosing make_counter call, so each counter keeps and updates its own n between calls.
wrong: global looks for n at module level, where none exists, and all counters would share one value.
Then n is reset to 0 on every call, so the counter always returns 1.
The name is not the problem; assigning to it is what makes it local to the inner function.

q: A generator expression doubles each score. It is passed to max(), then to list(), then to sum(). What does this print?
code:
scores = [3, 5, 8]
doubled = (s * 2 for s in scores)
print(max(doubled))
print(list(doubled))
print(sum(doubled))
options: TypeError: max() needs a list, not a generator
why: A generator produces each value once and is then exhausted. max() pulls all three values to find 16, so list() and sum() find nothing left: an empty list and 0. To reuse the values, build a list or create a new generator.
wrong: That needs the generator to restart, but it keeps its position and is used up after max().
list() already gets nothing; once exhausted, the generator yields no more values to any caller.
max(), list() and sum() accept any iterable, including generators.

q: numbers prints a message before each yield. What does this print?
code:
def numbers():
    print("start")
    yield 1
    print("middle")
    yield 2

g = numbers()
print("created")
print(next(g))
why: Calling a generator function only creates the generator; none of its body runs yet. next(g) runs the body up to the first yield, printing start and handing back 1. It pauses there, so middle is not printed.
wrong: numbers() does not run the body; it returns a paused generator, so created comes first.
The body is not run to the end up front; it runs only as values are requested.
After yielding 1 the generator pauses until the next next() call, so middle never prints.

q: for i in range(1_000_000_000) starts at once and uses almost no memory. Why?
options: range builds the full list, but in a background thread while the loop runs
Python stores runs of consecutive ints in a compressed list format
The interpreter skips the loop body until i is used for something
range keeps only start, stop and step and makes each number on demand
why: A range object is a small sequence that knows its start, stop and step. It computes each number when the loop asks for it, so its size does not grow with its length. list(range(n)) would build all n ints at once.
wrong: No list is ever built; range is its own lazy type, not a list made in the background.
There is no compression; the numbers are simply never stored together.
The body runs on every iteration; the saving comes from not storing the numbers.

q: A loop tries to double every price, then a list comprehension does the same. What does this print?
code:
prices = [10, 20, 30]
for p in prices:
    p = p * 2
print(prices)
doubled = [p * 2 for p in prices]
print(doubled)
why: p = p * 2 only rebinds the loop variable to a new int; the list still holds 10, 20, 30. The comprehension builds a new list from the results, which is how you get the doubled values.
wrong: The loop never changes prices, so the comprehension doubles the original values.
The loop variable is a name bound to each item; assigning to it does not write back into the list.
A comprehension does produce the doubled values; it returns a new list rather than changing prices.

q: names has 3 items and scores has 2. A loop runs over enumerate(zip(names, scores)). How many times does the body run, and what is the first index?
options: 3 times, with None as the last score
It raises ValueError because the lengths differ
why: zip pairs items until the shortest input runs out, so it yields 2 pairs and the extra name is dropped silently. enumerate counts from 0 unless you pass a start value.
wrong: zip stops at the shorter list, and enumerate starts at 0 unless given start=1.
zip does not pad missing values with None; it just stops at the shortest input.
Plain zip does not check lengths; it ends quietly when one input is exhausted.

q: This loop deletes every item with zero stock from a dict while iterating over it. What happens?
why: Deleting a key changes the dict's size while a loop is walking it, and Python stops that with RuntimeError. Loop over a snapshot such as list(stock), or build a new dict with a comprehension.
wrong: That is the intended result, but a dict refuses to change size during iteration, so the loop fails on the first delete.
That is the skipping seen with lists; a dict raises an error instead when its size changes in a loop.
del does remove the key; the trouble is that it happens while the dict is being iterated.

q: A Java developer expects this Python function to overflow: it returns the product of 1 to 30, which is far larger than 2**63. What does it return?
options: A negative number after the value wraps around
A float rounded to about 15 significant digits
The exact product, as a normal int
why: Python ints have no fixed width; they grow to hold any whole number, limited only by memory. So the product of 1 to 30 comes back exact. Very large ints are slower to work with, but they never wrap.
wrong: Wrapping happens with fixed-width ints such as Java's long; a Python int simply grows.
Int arithmetic does not overflow; OverflowError comes up in cases like converting a huge int to float.
The result stays an int; operations such as / are what turn values into floats.

q: A loop adds 0.1 to total ten times, and total == 1.0 is False. Which check should replace it?
options: Use round(total) == 1, which rounds away the error
Use math.isclose(total, 1.0), which allows a tiny gap
Use int(total) == 1, which drops the stray digits
Use str(total) == "1.0", since printing hides the error
why: 0.1 has no exact binary form, so each addition carries a tiny error and total ends up as 0.9999999999999999. Floats should be compared with a tolerance; math.isclose checks that two values are within a small relative gap.
wrong: round(total) == 1 also accepts totals like 0.6 or 1.4, so it hides real bugs.
int() cuts off the fraction, so 0.9999999999999999 becomes 0 and the check still fails.
str() shows the stored value, 0.9999999999999999, so the strings differ.

q: connect(timeout=None) fills in a missing value with if not timeout: timeout = 30. A caller passes timeout=0 to mean do not wait. What happens?
options: timeout stays 0, because 0 is a real value
A TypeError, because 0 is not None
why: not timeout is True for every falsy value: None, 0, 0.0, empty strings and empty containers. So 0 is treated as missing and replaced with 30. if timeout is None: checks only for the missing case.
wrong: if not checks truthiness, not whether a value was passed, and 0 is falsy.
Truth tests work on any value; no type check happens here.
The if branch assigns 30; nothing sets timeout back to None.

q: In Python, // is floor division (toward negative infinity), / gives a float, int() truncates toward zero, and % satisfies (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a. What does this print?
why: // rounds down toward negative infinity, so -7 // 2 is -4, not -3. The remainder takes the divisor's sign, which keeps (-7 // 2) * 2 + (-7 % 2) equal to -7, so it is 1. int() of -3.5 truncates toward zero, giving -3.
wrong: That is how C and Java divide, truncating toward zero. Python's // floors instead.
int() truncates toward zero instead of flooring, so int(-3.5) is -3.
If // gave -3, the remainder would have to be -1 to match; Python's // gives -4 and % gives 1.

q: increment is called twice on a Counter. What does this print?
why: Inside a method, count = ... creates a local variable that disappears when the method returns. Only self.count = self.count + 1 would update the attribute on the object, so c.count stays 0.
wrong: The new value goes into a local name, not onto the object, so both increments are lost.
No call updates self.count, so not even one increment sticks.
The right side reads self.count, which exists; the left side just creates a local.

q: In Python, looking up self.x falls back to the class if x is not on the instance, while assigning self.x writes an instance attribute. What does this print?
code:
class Player:
    badges = []
    score = 0

    def win(self, badge):
        self.badges.append(badge)
        self.score += 1

a, b = Player(), Player()
a.win("gold")
print(b.badges, b.score, a.score)
why: self.badges.append mutates the one list stored on the class, so b sees 'gold'. self.score += 1 reads the class value 0 and then assigns 1 to a new instance attribute on a only. b still reads the class's 0.
wrong: Both players share the class's single list; append changes it rather than giving a its own.
+= on an int assigns, and assigning through self creates an attribute on a only.
The shared list does change, and a.score += 1 stores 1 on a, so a.score reads 1.

q: A Point class defines __eq__ to compare x and y but does not define __hash__. What happens when code builds a set of Points?
options: Equal Points are merged into one entry
Equal Points are kept as separate entries
The set uses __eq__ for each lookup, so it runs in O(n)
why: Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes Python set __hash__ to None, so instances are unhashable and cannot go in a set or be dict keys. Defining both, with __hash__ built from the same fields, makes equal points merge.
wrong: Merging needs a hash that agrees with __eq__; without __hash__ the class cannot be hashed at all.
That is the Java result of overriding equals without hashCode. Python refuses instead.
A set always hashes first; with no hash there is no slow fallback, just the error.

q: Cart defines only __init__ and __len__. What does this print?
options: TypeError: object of type Cart has no len()
why: len(cart) calls cart.__len__(). With no __bool__, Python uses __len__ for truth tests too, so an empty cart is falsy and a cart with one item is truthy. Dunder methods are how a class plugs into built-in operations.
wrong: Objects are truthy by default only if they define neither __bool__ nor __len__; here __len__ returns 0.
len() works on any object whose class defines __len__.
bool() falls back to __len__ when __bool__ is missing.

q: load(source) only calls source.read(). A test passes an object of its own small class that has a read() method but is not a file. What happens?
options: It fails with a TypeError at once, because the argument is not a real file object
It works only if the class also defines every file method, such as write() and seek()
It works only after the test wraps the object with open() to turn it into a file
It works: load() only needs some object that has a read() method
why: Python looks for the method when the call happens; it does not check the object's class. Any object with a suitable read() works. This is duck typing, and it is why tests can pass simple fakes instead of real files.
wrong: Python does not check the type of an argument before using it; it only looks up read() when it is called.
Only the methods that are actually called matter. load() calls read(), so read() is all it needs.
open() takes a path or file descriptor, not an object. No wrapping is needed; having read() is enough.

q: Counting primes in pure Python is split across 4 threads on a 4-core machine, and it runs no faster than one thread. In standard CPython, what is the reason and the usual fix?
options: Threads start too slowly; reuse them with a thread pool
Only one thread runs Python code at a time; use processes
The OS gives each Python program a single core; raise its priority
The threads slow each other down on shared data; add a lock
why: Standard CPython has a global lock that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound pure Python code does not speed up with threads. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and can use all cores.
wrong: Startup cost is small next to the work; a pool would still run one thread's Python code at a time.
The OS can schedule threads on any core; the limit comes from the interpreter.
A lock adds safety, not speed; the threads would still take turns running Python code.

q: Standard CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) allowing one thread to run Python bytecode at a time. A script downloads 200 web pages, mostly waiting for network replies. Will threads help?
options: Yes, threads can wait on the network at the same time
No, the global lock lets only one thread run, so nothing overlaps
No, threads only help code written in C
Yes, but only if the machine has 200 cores
why: A thread that waits for I/O releases the interpreter lock, so other threads run in the meantime. The waits overlap and the total time drops sharply. The lock limits CPU work in Python code, not waiting.
wrong: The lock is released during blocking I/O, so many downloads can be in flight together.
Threads help any code that blocks on I/O, including pure Python code that calls the network.
Waiting does not use a core, so a few cores can serve many waiting threads.

q: A child process appends to the global list results, and the parent waits for it with join(). What does the parent print?
code:
from multiprocessing import Process

results = []

def work(n):
    results.append(n * n)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = Process(target=work, args=(3,))
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print(results)
options: RuntimeError: results is shared by two processes
why: Each process has its own memory. The child changes its own copy of results, and the parent's list stays empty. Results must be sent back explicitly, for example through a Queue or a Pool's return values.
wrong: Unlike threads, processes do not share globals; the child's append is invisible to the parent.
The work runs once, in the child, and even that append stays in the child's memory.
There is nothing shared to detect; each process quietly works on its own list.
